diagnostics.title: Universal baseline
diagnostics.summary: A short optional scan across DSA, core CS, systems, security, languages, AI/data, and operations.

domainRoadmaps.title: Foundations: reasoning before memorization
domainRoadmaps.summary: Build the shared language used in coding, data, systems, and behavioral interviews: complexity, data structures, algorithmic invariants, mathematics, SQL, Linux, networking, testing, and clear communication. The route starts with execution models and ends with timed interview synthesis.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: This track teaches the shared basics behind almost every technical interview: programming, problem solving, data, operating systems, networks, databases, and clear communication.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: These basics stop advanced topics from feeling like disconnected facts. They help you work out an answer even when you have never seen the exact interview question before.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of this track as learning the alphabet, grammar, and basic arithmetic of software. Every specialist subject builds sentences and calculations from these pieces.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Start with one small program and one array problem. Trace each line by hand, write down its time cost, and test an empty input before reading the advanced sections.

keyTerms.meaning: how the work or memory grows as the input grows
a way of arranging data for particular operations
a rule that must remain true while an algorithm runs

domainRoadmaps.audience: Use this route if fundamentals feel fragmented, if you are changing domains, or if solutions work but are difficult to explain, analyze, debug, or generalize under interview pressure.
outcomes: Analyze time and space costs from code rather than memorized labels.
Recognize the data-structure or algorithmic invariant behind a new problem.
Use probability, statistics, linear algebra, and discrete reasoning where the role requires them.
Query relational data and inspect Linux or network behavior with evidence.
Communicate assumptions, tests, trade-offs, and behavioral examples in a structured way.

stages.title: Programming and complexity
stages.plainEnglish: Learn what a program does one line at a time, how much work it performs, and how to find a bug using evidence instead of guesswork.
stages.objective: Develop a precise execution model for C++17, the STL, asymptotic analysis, testing, and debugging so every later solution can be explained in terms of operations, ownership, and evidence rather than syntax alone.
prerequisites: Basic programming syntax and a local C++17 toolchain
concepts: Trace stack, heap, value, reference, and iterator lifetimes.
Derive Big-O, Big-Theta, amortized cost, and practical constant factors.
Turn an example into boundary tests and a reproducible debugging hypothesis.
practice: Trace ten short programs before running them, then reconcile every wrong prediction.
Benchmark vector growth and hash-table lookup while separating asymptotic from measured behavior.
stages.deliverable: A small C++17 diagnostics repository with build commands, tests, debugger notes, complexity annotations, and a README explaining three bugs from symptom to root cause.
readinessGate: Derive nested-loop and recurrence costs without guessing.
Choose STL containers from operation requirements and invalidation rules.
Explain a failed test with a minimal reproduction and evidence.
interviewPrompts: Why can two O(n) implementations have materially different production performance?
What invalidates a vector iterator, and how would you prove that caused the crash?

stages.title: Linear structures and search patterns
stages.plainEnglish: Learn the most common containers and search patterns, then practise spotting which one fits a problem before you start coding.
stages.objective: Learn how contiguous storage, hashing, stacks, queues, linked structures, sorting, and binary search encode different invariants; practice recognizing signals before selecting a technique.
prerequisites: Programming and complexity stage completed
concepts: Maintain window, prefix, monotonic, and partition invariants.
Compare locality, resizing, collision, pointer, and ordering trade-offs.
Design examples that expose off-by-one errors, duplicates, and empty inputs.
practice: Solve one brute-force and one optimized problem per pattern, writing the invariant first.
Implement a hash map, queue, and binary-search boundary template with adversarial tests.
stages.deliverable: An annotated pattern notebook containing recognition signals, rejected approaches, invariants, complexity derivations, dry runs, and edge cases for at least twelve problems.
readinessGate: Explain why the chosen structure matches required operations.
Write lower-bound and upper-bound searches without boundary bugs.
Detect when hashing, sorting, or two pointers changes the trade-off.
interviewPrompts: When is sorting before scanning better than a hash table?
Prove that your binary-search loop cannot discard the answer.

stages.title: Trees, graphs, recursion, greedy, and DP
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how to explore choices and connections using trees, graphs, recursion, greedy reasoning, and dynamic programming.
stages.objective: Move from local operations to state spaces: represent hierarchical and network data, control recursive search, justify greedy choices, and derive dynamic programs from state and transition definitions.
prerequisites: Linear patterns and complexity fluency
concepts: Separate traversal order from graph representation and visited-state policy.
Derive backtracking and DP from choices, state, base cases, and transitions.
Use exchange arguments, cut properties, and counterexamples to validate greedy reasoning.
practice: Draw recursion trees and memoization state graphs before coding.
Solve equivalent graph problems with BFS, DFS, shortest path, and union-find where appropriate.
stages.deliverable: A pattern comparison dossier with one tree, graph, greedy, backtracking, and DP problem each, including proof sketches and a counterexample to a tempting wrong method.
readinessGate: State the DP state in one sentence before writing recurrence code.
Choose BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, or union-find from constraints.
Explain termination, completeness, and pruning in a search.
interviewPrompts: How do you discover a dynamic-programming state rather than memorize one?
Give a counterexample showing why a locally attractive greedy choice fails.

stages.title: Mathematics, SQL, Linux, and networking
stages.plainEnglish: Connect maths and SQL to the machine underneath so you can reason about data, processes, files, connections, and network delays.
stages.objective: Connect interview mathematics and data reasoning to the machines that execute queries and programs; build enough operational literacy to move between formula, query, process, file, socket, and packet.
prerequisites: Comfort with algebra, functions, and the command line
concepts: Translate probability and statistical claims into assumptions and uncertainty.
Reason about joins, grouping, nulls, cardinality, and query cost.
Trace name resolution, connections, processes, descriptors, and network hops.
practice: Solve probability cases by defining the sample space before calculating.
Write and explain SQL queries, then inspect process and network state with safe commands.
stages.deliverable: A reproducible investigation that loads a dataset, answers five SQL questions, measures query behavior, and documents the Linux process and network path used to serve the result.
readinessGate: Explain conditional probability without reversing the condition.
Predict join cardinality and null behavior before executing SQL.
Use process and network tools to narrow a fault layer by layer.
interviewPrompts: Why does correlation not establish causation, and what evidence would help?
A service is slow: how do you separate DNS, TCP, server, and database latency?

stages.title: Interview execution and revision
stages.plainEnglish: Turn your knowledge into a repeatable interview routine: clarify, plan, code, test, explain the cost, and communicate past experience clearly.
stages.objective: Convert knowledge into repeatable interview behavior: clarify the problem, communicate a plan, implement safely, test deliberately, discuss complexity, and tell concise behavioral stories with verifiable impact.
prerequisites: At least one completed problem and one systems investigation from each prior stage
concepts: Use a consistent clarify-plan-code-test-analyze loop.
Separate observations, assumptions, decisions, and results in explanations.
Build STAR stories around conflict, failure, ownership, learning, and impact.
practice: Run two timed coding mocks weekly and review recordings against a rubric.
Practice six behavioral stories with follow-up questions and quantified evidence.
stages.deliverable: A complete mock packet: coding transcript, self-score, corrected solution, six STAR story outlines, role questions, and a seven-day revision sheet.
readinessGate: Reach a correct approach before coding within the agreed timebox.
Test normal, boundary, invalid, and adversarial cases aloud.
Deliver each behavioral story in two minutes without losing the result.
interviewPrompts: Walk me through a time your first approach failed and how evidence changed it.
What do you do when you cannot see the optimal coding solution immediately?

capstone.title: Foundation interview loop
capstone.brief: Complete a ninety-minute simulation containing one coding problem, one SQL task, one systems diagnosis, and one behavioral question. Produce the implementation, reasoning transcript, test evidence, complexity analysis, and a written retrospective that prioritizes the next revision cycle.
evidence: Correct, tested code with an invariant and complexity derivation.
A SQL answer with null and cardinality reasoning.
A layer-by-layer diagnostic narrative using observable evidence.
A scored behavioral response and concrete improvement plan.

interviewLoop: Coding: two medium problems with clarification, invariant, tests, and complexity.
Core reasoning: probability, SQL, Linux, or networking follow-ups tied to evidence.
Debugging: locate a defect from symptoms and propose the smallest confirming experiment.
Behavioral: ownership, collaboration, failure, and learning with measurable outcomes.

misconceptions.claim: More problems always means better preparation.
misconceptions.correction: Unreviewed repetition hardens shallow pattern matching; deliberate review of recognition signals, invariants, errors, and alternate approaches creates transferable skill.

misconceptions.claim: Big-O predicts exact runtime.
misconceptions.correction: Asymptotic notation describes growth under a model; constants, cache locality, allocations, input distribution, and implementation still determine measured performance.

misconceptions.claim: A passing example proves correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Examples demonstrate behavior, while correctness needs an invariant or proof argument plus boundary and adversarial cases that could falsify the approach.

misconceptions.claim: Behavioral interviews require spontaneous authenticity.
misconceptions.correction: Authenticity and preparation are compatible: structured evidence helps a real experience remain concise, relevant, and easy for an interviewer to evaluate.

Explain one foundational, one interview-level, and one advanced trade-off without notes.
Rebuild the stage deliverables from a blank repository or blank document.

domainRoadmaps.title: AI + Data: from evidence to production decisions
domainRoadmaps.summary: Progress from data quality and statistical reasoning through classical machine learning, deep learning, transformers, retrieval, evaluation, and production ML systems. Every model choice is tied to a measurable objective, leakage-safe evaluation, operational constraints, and responsible failure handling.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: This track teaches you how to turn data into useful, tested decisions or AI features—from cleaning a table to training models and building LLM applications.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: AI interviews test more than model names. You must show that the data is trustworthy, the evaluation matches the goal, and the system still works outside a demo.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of AI work like scientific cooking: ingredients are the data, a recipe is the model, and a blind taste test is the evaluation. A fancy recipe cannot rescue spoiled ingredients.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Start with a small messy dataset. Describe every column, find missing or suspicious values, choose one simple question, and build the simplest baseline that can answer it.

keyTerms.meaning: an input value a model uses to make a prediction
a learned rule that maps inputs to an output
a controlled test of whether the result meets its goal

domainRoadmaps.audience: Use this route for AI engineering, ML engineering, data science, data engineering, MLOps, recommender, forecasting, computer-vision, NLP, and LLM-focused interview preparation.
outcomes: Turn a product question into measurable targets and valid experimental evidence.
Build and diagnose classical and deep-learning models from first principles.
Explain transformers, embeddings, retrieval, fine-tuning, and agent tool use precisely.
Design data, training, serving, evaluation, and monitoring systems together.
Identify leakage, bias, hallucination, drift, security, cost, and reliability risks.

stages.title: Data quality, EDA, and experiments
stages.plainEnglish: Before training anything, learn whether the data is trustworthy, what it can prove, and how a bad experiment can create a convincing wrong answer.
stages.objective: Learn to treat data as measured evidence with lineage, missingness, sampling, uncertainty, and causal limits before any model is selected or trained.
prerequisites: Foundational probability, statistics, SQL, and Python
concepts: Distinguish data-generating process from the observed table.
Prevent target, temporal, entity, and preprocessing leakage.
Design metrics, experiments, and slices that can falsify a hypothesis.
practice: Audit a messy dataset and write a leakage threat model before cleaning it.
Design an A/B test with unit, randomization, power, guardrails, and stopping rules.
stages.deliverable: A versioned analysis report containing a data contract, EDA, quality checks, experiment design, feature lineage, and a section on conclusions the evidence cannot support.
readinessGate: Explain every missing-value treatment from mechanism and downstream cost.
Separate exploratory findings from confirmatory claims.
Detect leakage from a pipeline diagram or suspicious validation result.
interviewPrompts: How can a perfectly implemented feature still leak future information?
When would an offline metric improvement fail to justify a product launch?

stages.title: Classical ML and evaluation
stages.plainEnglish: Build simple models first, compare them fairly, and choose measurements that match the real cost of a wrong prediction.
stages.objective: Build a strong baseline culture around linear, tree, and unsupervised models; connect objective functions, regularization, validation, calibration, thresholds, and business costs.
prerequisites: Evidence stage and foundational linear algebra
concepts: Connect loss geometry and optimization to model behavior.
Separate ranking, probability quality, thresholding, and business utility.
Diagnose bias, variance, imbalance, drift, and slice-specific failure.
practice: Implement linear and logistic models with gradients on a small dataset.
Compare a baseline and tree ensemble using nested, leakage-safe validation and calibration.
stages.deliverable: A model card and experiment ledger that records hypotheses, splits, baselines, metrics, slices, calibration, errors, uncertainty, and why the selected model beats alternatives.
readinessGate: Derive the selected loss and explain regularization effects.
Choose metrics from error costs instead of habit.
Explain why a validation protocol matches the deployment distribution.
interviewPrompts: Why can AUC improve while the deployed decision system becomes worse?
How do regularization, early stopping, and data augmentation differ?

stages.title: Deep learning and modalities
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how neural networks update themselves, then see how the same ideas are adapted for images, text, sequences, recommendations, and forecasts.
stages.objective: Understand backpropagation, representation learning, optimization, CNNs, sequence models, transformers, NLP, vision, recommenders, and forecasting as related architectures with modality-specific inductive biases.
prerequisites: Classical ML, optimization, calculus, and matrix operations
concepts: Trace tensor shapes, gradients, parameter sharing, and attention.
Match inductive bias to spatial, sequential, ranking, and temporal structure.
Diagnose optimization instability, overfitting, data shift, and evaluation mismatch.
practice: Manually trace forward and backward passes through a tiny network.
Train one modality model and perform structured error analysis across meaningful slices.
stages.deliverable: A reproducible training repository with seeded runs, data splits, baseline comparison, tensor-shape notes, experiment tracking, ablations, error slices, and an inference benchmark.
readinessGate: Explain attention and backpropagation without relying on framework magic.
Justify architecture and loss from data structure and objective.
Interpret a training failure from curves, gradients, examples, and data checks.
interviewPrompts: What does self-attention compute, and where does its quadratic cost come from?
How would you tell optimization failure from insufficient model capacity?

stages.title: Embeddings, RAG, fine-tuning, and agents
stages.plainEnglish: Build an LLM feature as a complete system: find information, construct context, generate an answer, use tools safely, and measure when it fails.
stages.objective: Design LLM applications as probabilistic systems with retrieval, context construction, tool boundaries, evaluation, security, latency, cost, and explicit abstention rather than prompt-only demos.
prerequisites: Transformers, information retrieval, APIs, and security basics
concepts: Separate retrieval, generation, orchestration, memory, and authorization.
Choose chunking, indexes, reranking, prompting, or tuning from measured failure modes.
Evaluate groundedness, relevance, task success, safety, latency, and cost.
practice: Build a small retrieval system with a labelled evaluation set and failure taxonomy.
Threat-model an agent with untrusted content, tools, credentials, and side effects.
stages.deliverable: An evaluated RAG or tool-using assistant with citations, abstention, authorization boundaries, trace logs, red-team cases, latency/cost measurements, and an improvement decision tree.
readinessGate: Diagnose retrieval failure separately from generation failure.
Explain when fine-tuning changes behavior but cannot add reliable knowledge.
Constrain tool calls with schemas, least privilege, validation, and confirmation.
interviewPrompts: When should you improve retrieval instead of changing the prompt or model?
How do you evaluate an agent whose path is nondeterministic?

stages.title: MLOps and ML system design
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how a model is versioned, deployed, watched, and rolled back so it remains useful after it leaves the notebook.
stages.objective: Join data, training, registry, deployment, inference, monitoring, governance, rollback, and human feedback into an evolvable system whose statistical and operational failures are observable.
prerequisites: One evaluated model or LLM application and basic distributed-systems knowledge
concepts: Version data, features, code, models, prompts, and evaluation sets together.
Design batch, streaming, online, and asynchronous inference around workload needs.
Monitor service health, input drift, outcome quality, fairness, and feedback delay.
practice: Draw an end-to-end ML system with ownership, contracts, and failure recovery.
Run a shadow or canary deployment exercise with rollback criteria and delayed labels.
stages.deliverable: A production design packet containing architecture, schemas, reproducibility plan, deployment strategy, SLOs, model-quality monitoring, governance, rollback, cost model, and incident playbook.
readinessGate: Trace one prediction back to versioned inputs and artifacts.
Separate data, concept, label, and operational drift.
Choose a deployment and feedback strategy from risk and label latency.
interviewPrompts: How would you detect a model failure before ground-truth labels arrive?
Design a recommendation or RAG platform for freshness, cost, and safe rollback.

capstone.title: Evidence-to-production AI system
capstone.brief: Build or design a complete AI product slice: define the decision and success measure, create leakage-safe data and evaluation, establish a baseline, train or integrate the model, expose inference, monitor statistical and operational health, and document security, responsible-AI, rollback, and cost trade-offs.
evidence: Versioned data, code, configuration, and evaluation artifacts.
Baseline and final model comparison with uncertainty and slices.
Architecture and failure-mode diagrams covering training and serving.
Model card, runbook, security review, and measured latency/cost report.

interviewLoop: Statistics and experimentation: assumptions, metrics, bias, uncertainty, and causal limits.
Modeling: derivation, objective, regularization, validation, errors, and trade-offs.
Coding and SQL: clean transformations, vectorization, testing, and data reasoning.
ML system design: data, training, serving, monitoring, security, cost, and rollback.
Applied case: clarify the product decision, establish a baseline, and propose an evaluation plan.

misconceptions.claim: A more complex model is a stronger baseline.
misconceptions.correction: A useful baseline is cheap, interpretable, reproducible, and hard to beat; complexity is justified only by measured value under the real evaluation and operating constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Cross-validation automatically prevents leakage.
misconceptions.correction: Validation only protects the split boundary when preprocessing, feature construction, entity grouping, and temporal availability are also fit or enforced inside each training fold.

misconceptions.claim: RAG guarantees factual answers.
misconceptions.correction: Retrieval can provide evidence, but the index may miss, retrieve irrelevant text, or contain stale or hostile content, and generation can still misstate the evidence.

misconceptions.claim: Production ML monitoring is ordinary service monitoring.
misconceptions.correction: Latency and errors are necessary but insufficient; statistical inputs, slices, decisions, delayed outcomes, calibration, and fairness also need explicit observability.

domainRoadmaps.title: SDE + Systems: code, runtime, and distributed trade-offs
domainRoadmaps.summary: Move from maintainable code and runtime internals through operating systems, databases, networks, backend engineering, distributed systems, reliability, and complete system-design cases. The route emphasizes invariants, failure boundaries, concurrency, data semantics, and explicit capacity assumptions.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: This track teaches how software is designed and how it behaves underneath: code structure, memory, concurrency, databases, networks, APIs, distributed systems, and system design.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Software-engineering interviews ask you to connect code to real behavior. You need to explain what happens when users, data, traffic, or failures increase—not only draw boxes.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of a software system as a city. Code defines individual buildings, APIs are entrances, networks are roads, databases are records offices, and operations keep the city usable.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Start by building one small API with one database table. Trace a request from the client to the server, through the query, and back to the response—including one failure.

keyTerms.meaning: a defined way for two software components to communicate
a group of data changes treated as one operation
a system whose parts run on multiple machines

domainRoadmaps.audience: Use this route for software, backend, full-stack, infrastructure, systems, fintech, data-platform, and architecture interviews that require both implementation fluency and design reasoning.
outcomes: Design testable modules and object models without mistaking patterns for goals.
Explain memory, concurrency, OS, database, and network behavior from first principles.
Build and evaluate APIs, backends, storage, caching, and event-driven systems.
Reason about consistency, partitioning, capacity, failure, and recovery.
Lead a system-design interview from requirements to bottlenecks and evolution.

stages.title: Code design, testing, and runtime
stages.plainEnglish: Learn to divide code into understandable parts, protect each part's rules, test behavior, and measure performance before changing the design.
stages.objective: Build reliable implementation instincts with OOP, SOLID, design patterns, modern C++ internals, ownership, testing strategy, and performance measurement.
prerequisites: Programming fundamentals and DSA basics
concepts: Model responsibilities, invariants, dependencies, and change boundaries.
Trace allocation, ownership, lifetime, dispatch, exceptions, and undefined behavior.
Use tests and profiles to replace design and performance guesses with evidence.
practice: Refactor a tightly coupled module behind explicit interfaces and characterization tests.
Profile and fix one memory or CPU bottleneck without changing externally visible behavior.
stages.deliverable: A small service or library with an architecture note, tests, benchmarks, ownership rules, and a before-and-after change showing why the design became easier to reason about.
readinessGate: Explain SOLID as change-risk heuristics rather than rigid laws.
Trace object and memory lifetime across a realistic call path.
Choose tests from failure risk and module boundaries.
interviewPrompts: When does dependency inversion add needless indirection?
How would you distinguish a memory leak from retained but reachable state?

stages.title: Concurrency, OS, databases, and networks
stages.plainEnglish: Follow one request through threads, memory, the operating system, the network, and the database so hidden behavior becomes easier to debug.
stages.objective: Understand the runtime substrate beneath applications: scheduling, synchronization, virtual memory, files, transactions, indexes, query plans, sockets, HTTP, and the ways concurrency and partial failure violate intuition.
prerequisites: Code design stage and foundational networking/SQL
concepts: Reason with happens-before, atomicity, isolation, and ownership.
Trace a request across process, socket, protocol, transaction, storage, and response.
Distinguish logical data guarantees from physical implementation mechanisms.
practice: Implement and test a bounded concurrent queue with a written synchronization argument.
Use query plans and network traces to diagnose a deliberately slow endpoint.
stages.deliverable: A request-path dossier with sequence diagrams, lock and transaction boundaries, query plans, packet-level observations, failure injection, and a corrected design.
readinessGate: Explain a race and its fix using ordering, not timing anecdotes.
Choose an isolation level from the business invariant.
Connect a latency symptom to a specific OS, network, or database experiment.
interviewPrompts: How can snapshot isolation still violate a business invariant?
What happens from clicking a URL to receiving the first response byte?

stages.title: APIs, backend architecture, and low-level design
stages.plainEnglish: Turn a product action into a clear API, business rule, database change, permission check, error response, and test.
stages.objective: Translate product behavior into contracts, domain models, persistence, authorization, idempotency, error semantics, deployment boundaries, and evolvable low-level designs.
prerequisites: Core runtime stage and one production language
concepts: Design API contracts around resources, operations, retries, and evolution.
Separate domain invariants from transport and persistence concerns.
Use sequence, state, class, and component diagrams to expose hidden decisions.
practice: Design and implement one idempotent write API with validation and tests.
Complete two LLD cases, then critique coupling, concurrency, and extension points.
stages.deliverable: A production-style API slice with specification, domain model, schema, migrations, authorization, idempotency, tests, observability, and an LLD rationale.
readinessGate: State invariants and concurrency boundaries before naming classes.
Explain retry and error behavior for every mutating endpoint.
Evolve an API or schema without breaking existing clients.
interviewPrompts: Design an idempotent create endpoint under client and server retries.
How do you keep domain rules from leaking across controllers, repositories, and jobs?

stages.title: Distributed data and reliability
stages.plainEnglish: Learn what changes when one program becomes many machines: messages can be late, duplicated, lost, stale, or handled by a failed component.
stages.objective: Design systems that remain understandable under scale and failure using partitioning, consistency, caching, queues, storage, capacity planning, reliability, and observability.
prerequisites: Backend stage and core database/networking fluency
concepts: Separate safety, liveness, availability, durability, and freshness guarantees.
Choose sync, async, cache, queue, replica, and partition boundaries from workload needs.
Design overload, retry, deduplication, backpressure, recovery, and observability together.
practice: Estimate a workload before drawing components, including peak and failure traffic.
Run a tabletop failure for duplicate events, a hot partition, stale cache, and regional loss.
stages.deliverable: A distributed service design with estimates, data model, consistency contract, partition plan, retry/deduplication policy, SLOs, dashboards, failure tests, and recovery sequence.
readinessGate: Quantify traffic, storage, bandwidth, and headroom assumptions.
Name the exact consistency and durability guarantee exposed to clients.
Show how the system degrades and recovers under dependency failure.
interviewPrompts: When is eventual consistency unsafe, and how can the product expose uncertainty?
Design a queue consumer that tolerates duplicates, poison messages, and overload.

stages.title: System-design synthesis
stages.plainEnglish: Practise a complete design interview from requirements and estimates to data, APIs, failures, security, monitoring, and trade-offs.
stages.objective: Practice a repeatable interview method that starts with user and business requirements, quantifies load, establishes data semantics, draws critical paths, tests failures, and evolves the design without premature complexity.
prerequisites: At least one deliverable from every prior SDE stage
concepts: Prioritize functional and non-functional requirements before architecture.
Drive the discussion through API, data, scale, reliability, security, and operations.
Use bottlenecks and changed assumptions to evolve a simple design.
practice: Complete one 45-minute design weekly with a written self-rubric.
Re-design the same system for ten-times scale, stricter consistency, and a regional outage.
stages.deliverable: Three complete case studies covering a feed or collaboration product, a payment or ledger system, and a high-volume observability or AI platform, each with estimates and failure analysis.
readinessGate: Reach a coherent baseline design before adding specialized infrastructure.
Defend each component with a requirement or measured constraint.
Identify the first bottleneck and an evidence-based evolution path.
interviewPrompts: Design a globally available service while preserving one named invariant.
Which requirement would make you remove the cache or queue from this design?

capstone.title: Production system design packet
capstone.brief: Design and prototype the critical path of a multi-user service. Include API and data contracts, concurrency and transaction invariants, capacity estimates, cache or event semantics, failure behavior, security boundaries, SLOs, observability, tests, and an evolution plan from one region to larger scale.
evidence: Working critical-path implementation with automated tests.
Architecture, sequence, state, and data-model diagrams.
Capacity worksheet and explicit consistency/durability contract.
Failure-injection results, dashboards, runbook, and design retrospective.

interviewLoop: Coding and debugging in the role's primary language.
Core CS: concurrency, OS, databases, networks, and runtime internals.
Low-level design: invariants, interfaces, extensibility, and tests.
System design: requirements, estimates, data, scale, failures, security, and operations.

misconceptions.claim: Design patterns are evidence of good design.
misconceptions.correction: A pattern is vocabulary for a recurring trade-off; good design is measured by clear responsibilities, protected invariants, testability, and the cost of likely changes.

misconceptions.claim: A distributed system is a larger single process.
misconceptions.correction: Independent clocks, partial failure, message delay, duplication, reordering, and split ownership create states that cannot occur in a single reliable process.

misconceptions.claim: Exactly-once delivery removes duplicate handling.
misconceptions.correction: Exactly-once claims hold within defined boundaries; side effects and cross-system workflows still need idempotency, deduplication, or transactional coordination.

misconceptions.claim: System design rewards the most components.
misconceptions.correction: Interview strength comes from a coherent baseline, explicit assumptions, quantified bottlenecks, and justified evolution, not from naming every infrastructure product.

domainRoadmaps.title: DevOps + Cloud: repeatable delivery and reliable operation
domainRoadmaps.summary: Build from Linux and network diagnosis through CI/CD, containers, infrastructure as code, Kubernetes, observability, SRE, incident response, platform engineering, cloud architecture, and cost control. Commands are treated as evidence-producing tools, not incantations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: This track teaches how software moves from a developer's machine into a reliable production environment using Linux, networks, pipelines, containers, cloud services, and operations.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: DevOps interviews test whether you can ship safely and recover calmly. Commands matter, but understanding what changed, how to observe it, and how to undo it matters more.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of DevOps as running a railway. Code is the passenger, pipelines are the route, infrastructure is the track, monitoring is the signal system, and rollback is the safe return path.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Start with one tiny web service. Run it locally, package it in a container, record its logs, deliberately break its configuration, and restore the last working version.

keyTerms.meaning: the process of releasing software into an environment
a measurable reliability target for a user-facing service
returning to a previously working version or state

domainRoadmaps.audience: Use this route for DevOps, platform, SRE, cloud, infrastructure, release, production engineering, and MLOps interviews across AWS, Azure, GCP, and OCI terminology.
outcomes: Diagnose Linux, DNS, TLS, routing, process, and resource failures systematically.
Design safe build, test, artifact, release, configuration, and secret flows.
Operate containers, Kubernetes, and infrastructure as code with recovery plans.
Define SLOs, observability, incidents, disaster recovery, and capacity controls.
Compare cloud services by responsibility, failure domain, security, and cost.

stages.title: Linux, shell, DNS, TLS, and networks
stages.plainEnglish: Learn the Linux and network path beneath a service so you can locate whether a failure is in the process, name lookup, connection, certificate, or application.
stages.objective: Develop a layer-by-layer operational model from process and filesystem through sockets, DNS, TLS, routing, load balancing, and production network paths.
prerequisites: Foundational Linux CLI and networking concepts
concepts: Use commands to test a specific hypothesis at a named layer.
Trace process, descriptor, namespace, cgroup, packet, name, and certificate state.
Write safe, idempotent shell automation with strict error handling.
practice: Diagnose a staged slow or unavailable service using process, socket, DNS, TLS, and HTTP evidence.
Write and test a shell health collector that never mutates the inspected system.
stages.deliverable: An operations notebook containing safe commands, expected outputs, interpretation, failure trees, and a complete diagnosis from alert to root cause.
readinessGate: Choose the next command from the current evidence.
Explain DNS caching and TLS identity boundaries.
Distinguish CPU, memory, disk, process, and network saturation.
interviewPrompts: A hostname works locally but fails in a container: how do you isolate the layer?
What evidence distinguishes a TLS trust failure from a name mismatch?

stages.title: GitOps, CI/CD, releases, config, and secrets
stages.plainEnglish: Build a safe path from a code change to production with tests, one versioned artifact, protected secrets, gradual release, and rollback.
stages.objective: Design a software supply path that converts reviewed source into immutable artifacts and controlled deployments with provenance, least privilege, rollback, and environment-safe configuration.
prerequisites: Runtime stage and Git/testing fundamentals
concepts: Separate source, build, artifact, configuration, secret, and deployment concerns.
Use quality gates, provenance, approvals, canaries, and rollback intentionally.
Model pipeline credentials and runners as production security boundaries.
practice: Build a pipeline that tests, scans, creates one immutable artifact, and promotes it.
Compare rolling, blue-green, canary, and feature-flag releases with failure drills.
stages.deliverable: A documented delivery pipeline with artifact provenance, environment promotion, secret boundaries, deployment verification, rollback automation, and a failed-release retrospective.
readinessGate: Prove the same artifact moves between environments.
Explain the rollback path for code, schema, and configuration.
Limit pipeline permissions and untrusted pull-request execution.
interviewPrompts: Why is rebuilding per environment weaker than promoting one artifact?
When can an automatic rollback make an incident worse?

stages.title: Containers, Kubernetes, and infrastructure as code
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how containers, Kubernetes, and infrastructure code describe the desired system and how to diagnose why reality differs from that description.
stages.objective: Understand images, namespaces, cgroups, reconciliation, scheduling, networking, storage, Terraform state, drift, and safe infrastructure change as converging desired-state systems.
prerequisites: Delivery stage and Linux/networking fluency
concepts: Trace desired state through controllers, plans, providers, and runtime objects.
Separate image, workload, network, storage, identity, and policy failures.
Design state, locking, drift detection, upgrades, and rollback for infrastructure.
practice: Containerize a service with non-root execution, health checks, and bounded resources.
Deploy it with Terraform and Kubernetes, then repair drift and a failed rollout.
stages.deliverable: A reproducible environment containing IaC modules, a Kubernetes workload, policy and secret boundaries, observability, upgrade notes, drift tests, and a teardown/recovery runbook.
readinessGate: Explain why a pod is pending, crashing, unready, or unreachable from evidence.
Predict a Terraform plan's effect on state and real infrastructure.
Design resource requests, limits, disruption, rollout, and rollback together.
interviewPrompts: What does Kubernetes reconcile, and why can desired state remain unmet?
How do you recover when Terraform state and real infrastructure disagree?

stages.title: Observability, SLOs, incidents, and disaster recovery
stages.plainEnglish: Learn to measure what users experience, create useful alerts, respond to incidents, and prove that backups and recovery actually work.
stages.objective: Turn telemetry into decisions using service objectives, symptom-based alerts, structured incident response, capacity and dependency awareness, and tested recovery objectives.
prerequisites: A deployed service and its delivery path
concepts: Connect metrics, logs, traces, profiles, events, and changes to user symptoms.
Use SLOs and error budgets to balance reliability and delivery risk.
Separate high availability, backup, restore, failover, continuity, and disaster recovery.
practice: Define SLIs and alerts for a service, then inject latency and dependency failure.
Run a restore or failover game day and measure actual RPO and RTO.
stages.deliverable: A reliability package with SLOs, dashboards, alerts, incident roles, timeline, postmortem, capacity forecast, backup verification, restore evidence, and prioritized follow-ups.
readinessGate: Every alert identifies an owner, impact, and first diagnostic action.
Demonstrate restore rather than only successful backup creation.
Explain error-budget policy and a concrete release decision.
interviewPrompts: Why can high CPU be a poor page while a latency SLI is a good one?
Design disaster recovery for a stateful service with explicit RPO and RTO.

stages.title: Cloud architecture and platform synthesis
stages.plainEnglish: Learn to choose and combine cloud services by the guarantees you need, then design a secure and affordable path that teams can operate.
stages.objective: Compare AWS, Azure, GCP, and OCI by primitives and responsibility boundaries, then design secure, reliable, observable, and cost-aware landing zones and developer platforms.
prerequisites: Platform and reliability stages plus IAM/security foundations
concepts: Map identity, network, compute, storage, database, observability, and governance primitives.
Choose managed versus self-managed services from control, skill, risk, and cost.
Treat platform APIs, paved roads, quotas, and tenancy as product design.
practice: Translate one architecture across all four cloud vocabularies without losing guarantees.
Design a paved-road service template with guardrails and an escape hatch.
stages.deliverable: A multi-cloud comparison and one detailed cloud design with account hierarchy, IAM, network, workloads, data, observability, resilience, cost model, and platform self-service workflow.
readinessGate: Explain shared responsibility for every managed service used.
Name failure domains, quotas, egress, lock-in, and recovery implications.
Defend platform abstractions with developer and operator outcomes.
interviewPrompts: How would the same private service architecture map across AWS, Azure, GCP, and OCI?
When is a managed platform worth higher unit cost and deeper vendor coupling?

capstone.title: Operable cloud platform
capstone.brief: Deliver a small service through an immutable CI/CD path into infrastructure defined as code and a container platform. Add identity, networking, secrets, policy, SLOs, telemetry, cost controls, failure injection, rollback, backup/restore, and an incident simulation with evidence.
evidence: Versioned pipeline, infrastructure, workload, and policy definitions.
Architecture and trust-boundary diagrams with cloud responsibility notes.
Dashboards, SLOs, alerts, incident timeline, and postmortem.
Measured rollback, restore, capacity, and cost results.

interviewLoop: Linux and networking troubleshooting from real command output.
CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes, Terraform, and cloud architecture design.
SRE: SLOs, observability, incidents, capacity, and disaster recovery.
Security and operations case: identity, secrets, supply chain, cost, and safe change.

misconceptions.claim: DevOps is a deployment toolchain.
misconceptions.correction: DevOps is a socio-technical operating model for fast, safe feedback across development and operations; tools help only when ownership, flow, and recovery improve.

misconceptions.claim: A green pipeline proves a safe release.
misconceptions.correction: Tests and scans reduce known risk, but runtime configuration, dependencies, data migrations, capacity, user behavior, and observability still determine release safety.

misconceptions.claim: Kubernetes fixes application reliability.
misconceptions.correction: Kubernetes can reconcile infrastructure and workload state, but it also adds distributed control planes and cannot repair unsafe application semantics or missing recovery design.

misconceptions.claim: Backups equal disaster recovery.
misconceptions.correction: Recovery requires valid, accessible backups plus practiced restore procedures, dependencies, credentials, capacity, routing, decision ownership, and measured RPO/RTO.

domainRoadmaps.title: Cybersecurity: model threats, enforce boundaries, prove response
domainRoadmaps.summary: Progress from risk, assets, trust boundaries, identity, cryptography, and secure design through web, API, network, cloud, container, Kubernetes, supply-chain, detection, incident response, and forensics. Security claims must be tied to an attacker model and verifiable control.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: This track teaches how systems are attacked and defended: threats, identity, cryptography, web and cloud security, secure development, detection, and incident response.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Security interviews reward clear reasoning about assets, attackers, boundaries, and evidence. Memorizing vulnerability names is not enough to choose or verify the right defense.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of security as protecting a building. First decide what matters, who may enter, where the doors are, how misuse is detected, and what happens after a break-in.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Start with a familiar login flow. Draw the user, browser, server, and database; mark where trust changes; then list one attack and one testable defense at each boundary.

keyTerms.meaning: a possible harmful action by an attacker or event
a weakness that can allow harm to occur
a safeguard that prevents, detects, or limits harm

domainRoadmaps.audience: Use this route for security engineering, AppSec, cloud security, DevSecOps, product security, detection, incident response, and security-aware software or infrastructure interviews.
outcomes: Turn an architecture into assets, trust boundaries, abuse cases, and prioritized controls.
Explain identity, authorization, cryptography, PKI, and protocol guarantees precisely.
Find and prevent web, API, network, code, cloud, and supply-chain weaknesses.
Design detection and response around evidence, containment, and recovery.
Communicate residual risk, assumptions, control coverage, and validation plans.

stages.title: Foundations and threat modeling
stages.plainEnglish: Start by deciding what needs protection, who might attack it, where trust changes, and which defenses reduce the most meaningful risk.
stages.objective: Learn to reason from assets, actors, trust boundaries, attack paths, likelihood, impact, and verifiable mitigations instead of applying security checklists without context.
prerequisites: Foundational networking, operating systems, and software architecture
concepts: Distinguish threat, vulnerability, exploit, control, exposure, and risk.
Use data-flow diagrams and abuse cases to find boundary crossings.
Prioritize controls by attacker effort, impact, detectability, and residual risk.
practice: Threat-model a familiar login and data-export flow from a diagram.
Map controls to OWASP or NIST outcomes while preserving system-specific reasoning.
stages.deliverable: A threat model with assets, actors, data flows, trust boundaries, prioritized abuse cases, mitigations, validation steps, owners, and explicitly accepted residual risks.
readinessGate: Every mitigation addresses a named attack path.
Separate prevention, detection, response, and recovery controls.
State assumptions and update the model when architecture changes.
interviewPrompts: What makes a threat model actionable rather than a STRIDE checklist?
How do you prioritize two high-severity findings with different exploitability and exposure?

stages.title: Identity, authorization, cryptography, and PKI
stages.plainEnglish: Learn the difference between proving identity, granting permission, protecting data, verifying messages, and managing keys over time.
stages.objective: Build exact mental models for authentication, sessions, federation, authorization, keys, hashes, signatures, encryption, certificates, TLS, rotation, revocation, and failure recovery.
prerequisites: Risk modeling and network protocol fundamentals
concepts: Separate identity proof, authentication, session, authorization, and audit.
Choose primitives from confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation needs.
Manage keys and credentials across generation, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and recovery.
practice: Trace an OAuth/OIDC or service-identity flow and mark every trust decision.
Inspect a certificate chain and explain each TLS failure from evidence.
stages.deliverable: An identity and cryptography design for users and services with flows, policies, token/session handling, key lifecycle, certificate validation, logging, and recovery from credential compromise.
readinessGate: Explain hashing, MACs, signatures, and encryption without conflating them.
Enforce least privilege with server-side authorization at each resource boundary.
Describe rotation and revocation without assuming instant global state.
interviewPrompts: Why does a valid token not prove an action is authorized?
What does TLS authenticate, and what does it leave to the application?

stages.title: Web, API, network, and secure coding
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how common web, API, and network attacks cross a boundary, then fix the correct boundary and prove the weakness stays closed.
stages.objective: Apply threat models to parsers, browsers, APIs, networks, code, dependencies, and business workflows; focus on input boundaries, output contexts, authorization, state, and safe failure.
prerequisites: Identity and cryptography stage plus backend and network basics
concepts: Distinguish injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, traversal, deserialization, and auth failures.
Treat business logic, object ownership, rate limits, and replay as security boundaries.
Prioritize vulnerability work by reachability, exploitability, asset value, and compensating controls.
practice: Review a small API for object-level authorization, injection, replay, and unsafe errors.
Build a safe proof of concept in a local lab and write remediation plus regression tests.
stages.deliverable: An AppSec assessment containing architecture, attack surface, validated findings, risk rationale, minimal reproductions, fixes, tests, logging recommendations, and residual risk.
readinessGate: Explain source, sink, control, and exploit preconditions for each finding.
Propose fixes at the correct trust boundary rather than only filtering input.
Write a regression test that proves the vulnerability stays closed.
interviewPrompts: Why is input validation insufficient as the only defense against XSS?
How do you distinguish authentication failure from broken object authorization?

stages.title: Cloud, containers, Kubernetes, and supply chain
stages.plainEnglish: Protect the path from source code to a running cloud workload, including build systems, dependencies, images, identities, secrets, and policies.
stages.objective: Secure identities, control planes, workloads, images, clusters, build systems, artifacts, dependencies, secrets, and provenance across shared-responsibility boundaries.
prerequisites: Application security plus cloud/container fundamentals
concepts: Map human, workload, pipeline, and control-plane identities and permissions.
Reduce build-to-runtime attack surface with provenance and policy.
Separate host, image, orchestration, network, data, and application controls.
practice: Review an IaC and Kubernetes deployment for identity, network, secret, and policy risks.
Model a dependency or pipeline compromise and design containment plus provenance checks.
stages.deliverable: A hardened delivery and runtime design with least-privilege identities, signed artifacts, SBOM/provenance, admission policy, secret handling, segmentation, logging, and compromise recovery.
readinessGate: Explain the shared-responsibility boundary for each managed layer.
Trace source-to-runtime provenance for one artifact.
Contain a compromised workload without trusting the workload itself.
interviewPrompts: What does image signing prove, and what does it not prove?
How can a CI runner compromise production without direct production credentials?

stages.title: Detection, incident response, and forensics
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how to notice a likely attack, collect reliable evidence, limit the damage, restore service, and improve the system afterward.
stages.objective: Design evidence collection, high-signal detections, triage, containment, eradication, recovery, and learning while preserving timelines and forensic integrity.
prerequisites: Threat models and telemetry from at least one application or cloud system
concepts: Connect threat hypotheses to observable events and expected false positives.
Preserve identity, time, provenance, and chain of custody in evidence.
Balance containment speed with business impact and evidence preservation.
practice: Write and test three detections against benign and malicious event sets.
Run a tabletop incident from alert through recovery and post-incident control changes.
stages.deliverable: An incident case file with detection logic, triage evidence, timeline, scope, containment decisions, forensic notes, recovery validation, communication plan, and lessons mapped back to the threat model.
readinessGate: Explain why the alert is actionable and how it can fail.
Build a defensible timeline from correlated sources.
Verify eradication and recovery rather than assuming containment ended the incident.
interviewPrompts: How do you tune a noisy detection without creating a blind spot?
What evidence would change your containment decision during an active incident?

capstone.title: Threat-to-response security review
capstone.brief: Assess a realistic web or cloud system end to end: model assets and abuse paths, review identity and crypto, validate application and infrastructure controls, design telemetry and detections, simulate one compromise, preserve evidence, and produce prioritized remediation plus recovery verification.
evidence: Threat model and trust-boundary diagrams.
Validated findings with safe reproductions and regression tests.
Hardened design, policy, provenance, and detection artifacts.
Incident timeline, containment rationale, recovery evidence, and residual-risk register.

interviewLoop: Security foundations: threat models, IAM, cryptography, PKI, and protocols.
Application or cloud review: identify attack paths and propose testable mitigations.
Detection and incident case: interpret evidence, scope impact, contain, and recover.
Coding or automation: parse data, validate inputs, inspect logs, or enforce policy safely.

misconceptions.claim: Compliance means the system is secure.
misconceptions.correction: Frameworks establish control expectations and evidence, while security still depends on the actual threat model, implementation, exposure, validation quality, and residual risk.

misconceptions.claim: Encryption protects data from every privileged component.
misconceptions.correction: Encryption protects against specific observers and access paths; endpoints, keys, authorized services, metadata, memory, and compromised identities can remain exposed.

misconceptions.claim: Zero trust means trusting nothing.
misconceptions.correction: Zero trust replaces implicit network trust with continuous, explicit decisions based on identity, device, workload, policy, context, and observable risk.

misconceptions.claim: Incident response ends after containment.
misconceptions.correction: Eradication, recovery validation, monitoring, communication, evidence preservation, root-cause analysis, and durable control changes are required to close the incident.

domainRoadmaps.title: Fintech + Quant: preserve money and model uncertainty
domainRoadmaps.summary: Learn exact monetary representation, double-entry ledgers, idempotent payment workflows, reconciliation, settlement, fraud, compliance, resilience, market microstructure, stochastic models, derivatives, portfolios, backtesting, and low-latency engineering. Financial invariants and auditability lead every design.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: This track has two connected sides: building software that moves and records money safely, and using mathematics and data to reason about markets, pricing, and risk.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Financial interviews care about exactness. A duplicated payment, an unbalanced ledger, or a biased backtest can look successful while producing a serious real-world loss.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of fintech as a chain of signed receipts and quant work as testing a measuring instrument. Every amount needs a traceable history, and every model needs known limits.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Start with a tiny double-entry ledger that transfers ₹100 between two accounts. Repeat the same request twice and prove the money moves only once while the history remains visible.

keyTerms.meaning: the authoritative history of financial entries and balances
making repeated identical requests produce one lasting effect
the final transfer of value between participating institutions

domainRoadmaps.audience: Use this route for fintech engineering, payments, banking, lending, risk, fraud, trading systems, quant development, and quantitative research interviews, with India-first regulatory context.
outcomes: Represent money and accounting events without losing value or audit history.
Design retry-safe payments, cards, UPI, banking, lending, settlement, and reconciliation flows.
Explain compliance, fraud, security, resilience, and regulatory boundaries.
Reason about markets, time series, stochastic processes, pricing, portfolios, and risk.
Avoid backtesting bias and design measurable low-latency systems.

stages.title: Money, ledgers, and idempotency
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how to represent money exactly, record every movement with balanced entries, and make retries safe without erasing history.
stages.objective: Establish the invariants beneath financial systems: exact value representation, currencies and rounding, balanced postings, immutable history, account states, retries, reversals, and audit trails.
prerequisites: SQL, transactions, integer arithmetic, and API basics
concepts: Separate business event, payment state, ledger transaction, and balance view.
Preserve zero-sum postings, currency, scale, ordering, and traceability.
Design idempotency scope, key lifecycle, conflict behavior, and safe retry responses.
practice: Implement a small append-only double-entry ledger with invariant tests.
Simulate duplicate, delayed, reordered, and partially failed requests.
stages.deliverable: A ledger prototype with posting rules, balances derived from entries, idempotent command handling, reversals, audit queries, concurrency tests, and invariant documentation.
readinessGate: Prove every accepted transaction balances by currency.
Correct errors with compensating entries rather than history mutation.
Return the original outcome for a valid duplicate request.
interviewPrompts: Why is a mutable balance column insufficient as the financial source of truth?
How should an idempotency key behave when the payload changes?

stages.title: Payments, cards, UPI, banking, and lending
stages.plainEnglish: Follow a payment across users, banks, card or UPI networks, callbacks, timeouts, refunds, and the final movement of money.
stages.objective: Model multi-party workflows as explicit state machines with authorization, capture, clearing, settlement, mandates, refunds, disputes, timeouts, callbacks, and compensating actions.
prerequisites: Money and ledger stage plus networking and API design
concepts: Separate user intent, orchestration, rail message, ledger effect, and external settlement.
Handle ambiguous outcomes, asynchronous callbacks, retries, and human operations.
Model lending schedules, interest, delinquency, and servicing with exact contracts.
practice: Draw card and UPI flows with actors, states, timeouts, and ledger entries.
Design a payment API and webhook consumer resilient to duplicates and reordering.
stages.deliverable: A payment-or-lending design packet with state machines, APIs, ledger postings, retry rules, webhook verification, timeout recovery, disputes, and support-facing audit views.
readinessGate: Name every terminal, retryable, pending, and ambiguous state.
Reconcile external events to internal intent and postings.
Explain what the user sees while the true external outcome is unknown.
interviewPrompts: How do you resolve a payment timeout when the provider may have succeeded?
Where do authorization, capture, clearing, and settlement differ?

stages.title: Reconciliation, settlement, fraud, compliance, and resilience
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how teams find missing money, handle settlement breaks, reduce fraud, meet compliance duties, and recover without losing the audit trail.
stages.objective: Operate financial workflows safely by comparing independent records, explaining breaks, controlling fraud, meeting KYC/AML and PCI obligations, and recovering without losing auditability.
prerequisites: Payment rails stage and security/reliability fundamentals
concepts: Use independent books and deterministic matching to detect missing or inconsistent value.
Balance fraud loss, customer friction, model uncertainty, and manual review.
Treat compliance controls, evidence, access, retention, and recovery as system requirements.
practice: Reconcile internal ledger, processor report, and bank statement with controlled breaks.
Run a fraud or settlement incident tabletop including customer and regulatory communication.
stages.deliverable: An operations console design with reconciliation rules, break queues, case evidence, fraud decisions, access controls, settlement positions, escalation paths, and disaster-recovery tests.
readinessGate: Every monetary break has an owner, reason, amount, age, and resolution trail.
Fraud thresholds are tied to cost, calibration, and review capacity.
Recovery preserves ledger invariants and external reconciliation.
interviewPrompts: Why can two internally consistent ledgers still disagree with settlement?
How would you tune fraud controls when false positives block valuable customers?

stages.title: Markets, probability, pricing, portfolios, and risk
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how orders create markets and how probability, time series, pricing, portfolios, and risk models describe uncertain financial outcomes.
stages.objective: Build quantitative reasoning from order-book mechanics and stochastic processes through time-series assumptions, derivative pricing, portfolios, and risk measures without hiding model limits.
prerequisites: Probability, statistics, calculus, linear algebra, and programming
concepts: Connect orders, matching, liquidity, spread, impact, and market data.
State stochastic and time-series assumptions before deriving or estimating.
Distinguish pricing measure, real-world probability, hedge, exposure, and risk metric.
practice: Reconstruct an order book and compute spread, depth, and simple impact.
Derive and simulate one stochastic model, then test sensitivity to violated assumptions.
stages.deliverable: A quantitative notebook with market-data cleaning, order-book metrics, model derivation, simulation, parameter estimation, pricing or risk outputs, sensitivity analysis, and assumption failures.
readinessGate: Derive a result with dimensions and limiting cases checked.
Explain model risk and the scenario that invalidates the estimate.
Separate prediction, pricing, hedging, and risk measurement objectives.
interviewPrompts: Why is volatility not the same as risk?
What assumptions make a pricing or time-series model tractable, and how do they fail?

stages.title: Backtesting, low latency, security, and regulation
stages.plainEnglish: Learn how to test a strategy without using future information and how to build fast financial software without sacrificing correctness or recovery.
stages.objective: Turn strategies and financial services into defensible production systems by eliminating look-ahead and survivorship bias, modeling costs, measuring latency, securing data, and labeling jurisdiction-specific obligations.
prerequisites: Markets/models or payment operations stage plus performance and security engineering
concepts: Separate research data, signal time, decision time, execution, fill, and evaluation.
Measure latency distributions, allocations, contention, serialization, network, and I/O.
Record jurisdiction, effective date, source, applicability, and legal-review boundary.
practice: Backtest a simple strategy with walk-forward validation, costs, and leakage checks.
Profile a market-data or payment critical path and document every optimization trade-off.
stages.deliverable: A research-to-production dossier with bias controls, cost/slippage model, out-of-sample evidence, performance profile, operational controls, regulatory source register, and kill/rollback procedure.
readinessGate: Prove no feature or universe uses future information.
Report latency percentiles and worst-path causes, not only averages.
Label regulatory claims by jurisdiction and review date.
interviewPrompts: How can a profitable backtest be entirely invalid?
Which low-latency optimization would you reject because it weakens correctness or recovery?

capstone.title: Auditable financial system
capstone.brief: Design either a payment/ledger service or a quantitative research-to-execution workflow. Preserve exact value and temporal semantics, model retries and external ambiguity, add reconciliation, risk and fraud controls, security, observability, recovery, performance evidence, and jurisdiction-labelled compliance notes.
evidence: State machines, APIs, schemas, ledger or position invariants, and tests.
Reconciliation, audit, fraud/risk, access, and incident workflows.
Performance, capacity, failure, recovery, and cost measurements.
Assumption register and date-stamped regulatory source map.

interviewLoop: Financial engineering: money, ledgers, idempotency, payments, reconciliation, and audit.
Systems design: scale, consistency, security, resilience, external ambiguity, and operations.
Quantitative reasoning: probability, markets, time series, pricing, portfolio risk, or puzzles.
Coding: exact arithmetic, state transitions, data processing, C++ performance, SQL, or Python research.

misconceptions.claim: A successful API response means money settled.
misconceptions.correction: Responses often acknowledge an internal state transition; authorization, capture, clearing, settlement, reconciliation, refunds, and disputes are distinct events with different finality.

misconceptions.claim: Double entry means storing debit and credit columns.
misconceptions.correction: Double entry is an accounting invariant across postings and accounts; the data model must preserve balanced, immutable, explainable economic events rather than merely name two fields.

misconceptions.claim: A high backtest Sharpe proves a strategy.
misconceptions.correction: Leakage, multiple testing, survivorship, regime selection, costs, market impact, capacity, unstable parameters, and operational failure can manufacture or erase apparent performance.

misconceptions.claim: Regulatory requirements are globally interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: Terms may look similar, but applicability, obligations, reporting, consent, retention, and enforcement vary by jurisdiction, entity, product, and effective date.

rolePaths.title: Frontend Engineer
rolePaths.summary: Master the browser platform, accessible interface engineering, typed component design, state and data flow, performance, security, testing, and delivery rather than preparing as a framework-only developer.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: A frontend engineer builds the part of a website or web application that people see, click, type into, and use.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: You need browser, accessibility, state, performance, and testing knowledge so the interface works for real people—not only in a perfect demo.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of frontend work as designing and operating a shop floor: users need clear signs, fast service, accessible paths, and useful recovery when something goes wrong.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Build one accessible form with validation, loading, success, and error states before adding a large framework architecture.

keyTerms.meaning: a reusable piece of an interface
data that determines what the interface currently shows
making the interface usable across abilities and input methods

rolePaths.reason: Frontend Engineer interviews combine shared computer-science reasoning, stack-specific implementation, production trade-offs, debugging evidence, design communication, and a project that proves the candidate can connect those layers.
outcomes: Trace HTML, CSS, browser rendering, events, and JavaScript execution.
Model UI state, server state, ownership, and component boundaries explicitly.
Build keyboard and screen-reader access into semantics before styling.
Design resilient client-server contracts with loading, empty, error, retry, and stale states.
Test behavior at unit, integration, browser, visual, and accessibility boundaries.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: An AI engineer builds product features around models, retrieval, tools, evaluation, safety, serving, and user feedback.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: The role turns a model demo into a dependable product. You must know which part failed, measure quality, control tool access, and manage latency and cost.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of an AI application as a junior researcher with a library and tools: it can be useful, but needs good sources, clear permissions, checking, and a safe way to say 'I don't know.'
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Build a tiny question-answering feature over five documents. Create ten labelled questions, require citations, record failures, and fix retrieval before changing the model.
